Fractures of the distal tibial articular surface

TibialPilon

A high-energy, intra-articular fracture of the weight-bearing distal tibia — hostile to the soft-tissue envelope and unforgiving even when the reduction is anatomic. Named by Destot in 1911, redefined by Rüedi & Allgöwer, then transformed by the staged revolution of the 1990s.

Mechanism

01 — AXIAL LOAD

Most pilons are an axial explosion: the talus is rammed into the plafond. The position of the foot at the instant of impact decides which part of the joint shatters. A lower-energy rotational variant — a spiral shaft fracture running into the joint — leaves larger fragments and a kinder prognosis.

  • Neutral / plantigrade → central articular depression
  • Dorsiflexed → anterior plafond fragment
  • Plantarflexed → posterior plafond fragment

Classification

02 — RÜEDI & AO/OTA

Two languages. Rüedi–Allgöwer grades articular displacement and comminution (I → III) and carries prognosis. OTA/AO 43 sorts by joint involvement — A extra-articular, B partial (a constant fragment stays with the shaft), C complete (nothing constant to build on). Hover a row to preview the plate.

Three Columns

03 — PATHOANATOMY

Assal's three-column model drives approach and plate placement. Ligaments usually survive, tethering three recurring CT fragments — medial malleolar, Chaput (anterolateral), Volkmann (posterolateral). Secure every column or the construct fails in the coronal plane.

COLUMN 01

Medial Column

Diaphysis to the medial malleolus. Buttress here or it collapses into varus.

COLUMN 02

Lateral Column

Anterolateral tibia + the fibula — 20–30% of load, and the key to length & rotation.

COLUMN 03

Posterior Column

Posterior tibia tied to the fibula by Volkmann. In 43C it dissociates entirely.

COLUMN 04

One Plate Never Holds

Anterolateral plate → add medial. Medial plate → add anterior. Fix the fibula.

Approach Atlas

04 — SCROLL TO TRAVEL

Choose by fragment location, the columns involved, and the state of the skin. Aim for a 7 cm skin bridge between parallel incisions, never under 5 cm. Scroll to travel the atlas; full detail follows below.

Anteromedial

Fig 64-17

Workhorse for medial & central plafond and the medial malleolus.

IncisionFrom the mid-distal third just lateral to the crest, running distal medial to the anterior tibial tendon. The extensile modification stays straight and does not curve around the medial malleolus.
IntervalFollow and mobilise the anterior tibial tendon laterally; enter the joint through existing capsular tears to spare the envelope.
At riskAnterior tibial tendon sheath (repairable), saphenous vein & nerve anteromedially.
FixationMedial buttress plate; add a small anterior plate if there is AP comminution.

Anterior (straight)

standard

Access to the whole plafond — medial, central and the Chaput tubercle.

IncisionMidline over the ankle; a true midline lets you add posteromedial and posterolateral incisions 120° apart.
IntervalMove the neurovascular bundle and EHL laterally, tibialis anterior medially.
At riskSuperficial peroneal nerve; dorsalis pedis / deep peroneal bundle.
FixationCentral articular reconstruction then span to the shaft with column plates.

Anterolateral

Fig 64-19

Anterolateral / central plafond and the Chaput fragment; allows fibular plating.

Incision~5 cm proximal to the joint, just medial to Chaput, toward the 3rd–4th metatarsal bases.
IntervalDivide the extensor retinaculum; sweep EDL, peroneus tertius, deep peroneal nerve and dorsalis pedis medially.
At riskSuperficial peroneal nerve in the subcutaneous plane.
FixationAnterolateral plate; approach is non-extensile so proximal screws go percutaneously, and a medial plate needs its own incision — an isolated anterolateral plate fails in varus.

Posterolateral

Fig 64-20

Posterior malleolar free fragment (C-type) and the fibula through one incision.

IncisionVertical, midway between the lateral border of the Achilles and the posterolateral fibula.
IntervalMedial to the peroneal tendons; through the lateral fibres of FHL to the posterior column.
At riskSural nerve & lesser saphenous vein.
FixationPosterior buttress plate; the joint is reduced indirectly off the posterior cortical read.

Posteromedial

Fig 64-21

Posteromedial fragment, tendon / NV entrapment, and tarsal-tunnel release.

IncisionJust medial to the Achilles, between it and the posteromedial tibia.
IntervalRetract FHL; identify and protect the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle.
At riskPosterior tibial artery & tibial nerve.
FixationPosteromedial buttress; ideal when tendons or the NV bundle block reduction.

Mod. posteromedial

Fig 64-22

Wide access to the whole posterior metaphysis via the deep posterior compartment.

IncisionMedial to the Achilles, dissecting to the transverse intermuscular septum.
IntervalTibial nerve runs along the medial border of FHL; work between deep compartment structures.
At riskTibial nerve, posterior tibial vessels.
FixationBroad posterior buttress for comminuted posterior metaphyseal patterns.

Staged Protocol

05 — SPAN · SCAN · PLAN

The modern standard for high-energy pilons is two stages: temporise, let the envelope recover, then reconstruct. Definitive ORIF waits until the wrinkle sign returns — usually beyond ten days.

  • DAY 0

    Emergency Dept

    Splint off, reduce gross deformity with gentle traction to protect tented skin. Document pulses and sensation; antibiotics and sterile dressing if open. Read the blisters — clear lance-able, blood-filled left to eschar.

  • DAY 0–1

    Stage I · Ex-Fix

    Ankle-spanning delta frame, pins clear of future incisions, ± fibular plating if you are the definitive surgeon. Restore length, alignment and rotation — do not overdistract.

  • DAY 1–2

    Scan

    CT only after the frame is on and the limb is out to length. Map the Chaput, Volkmann and impacted fragments and the talar dome; the CT dictates incisions and plate strategy.

  • ~1 WEEK

    Interval

    Soft tissues rest and recover. Wait for the wrinkle sign and for blisters to re-epithelialise before committing to definitive incisions.

  • ~2–3 WK

    Stage II · ORIF

    Once the envelope tolerates it, reconstruct the articular surface posterior→anterior, hold with a K-wire jail, and buttress each column; graft metaphyseal voids.

  • ~6 WK

    Wound watch

    Sutures left up to six weeks anteriorly. Treat superficial slough with local care; take exposed tendon or bone straight back to theatre.

  • ~12 WK

    Weight-bearing

    Progressive load with radiographic healing. Counsel that arthritis can still follow an anatomic reduction — the cartilage was injured at impact.

Complications

06 — THE LONG TAIL

Soft-tissue problems lead, then bone and joint. The envelope is the enemy early; malalignment and arthritis are the enemy late.

01

Superficial necrosis

Dry eschar; local care. Erythema is usually inflammatory, not infection.

02

Deep slough

Exposed tendon/bone → admit, I&D, retain stable implants, VAC, flap.

03

Osteomyelitis

Cierny–Mader host/anatomy. Debride to the paprika sign; 6 wk antibiotics.

04

Nonunion ≤16%

Metadiaphyseal, usually varus + medial shortening. Mechanical, not biologic.

05

Posttraumatic OA

Can follow an anatomic reduction. Keep the limb aligned for any future fusion.
